sourceLine: RAW as the true dependence, WAR and WAW as name collisions that an in-order pipeline cannot trip over, and renaming as their fix: Sarangi chapter 10, section 10.4.2 and 10.11.4 (English, read in full). The RAW/WAR/WAW table with an example of each: DSWallah Learn 'Pipeline Hazards & Stalls', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Data Hazards: RAW, WAR and WAW, and Which Ones Actually Stall
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: Three name collisions are possible between instructions: RAW (a later instruction reads what an earlier one writes - a true dependence), WAR (a later instruction writes what an earlier one reads - an anti-dependence) and WAW (two writes to one register - an output dependence). In an in-order pipeline only RAW can go wrong.
remember: RAW is the true dependence: the value must exist before it is read, so the reader must wait or the value must be forwarded.
In an in-order pipeline a preceding instruction is always ahead of a succeeding one, so every read happens before any later write: WAR and WAW cannot produce a wrong value and do not stall.
WAR and WAW become real in out-of-order and multiple-issue machines, where a later instruction may pass an earlier one; register renaming removes them.
Classify a pair by the earlier access first: write then read is RAW, read then write is WAR, write then write is WAW, read then read is nothing at all.
GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.16 asks which of the four dependencies can cause a data hazard: only read-after-write.

example.prompt: I1: DIV R3, R1, R2; I2: SUB R5, R3, R4; I3: ADD R3, R5, R6; I4: MUL R7, R3, R8. Which statements hold - RAW on R3 between I1 and I2, WAR on R3 between I1 and I3, RAW on R3 between I2 and I3, WAW on R3 between I3 and I4?
example.work: Write R3 sets: I1 writes, I2 reads, I3 writes, I4 reads. I1 writes then I2 reads: RAW, true. I1 writes and I3 writes: WAW, so the WAR claim is false. I2 reads and I3 writes: that is WAR, so the RAW claim is false. I3 writes and I4 reads: RAW, so the WAW claim is false.
example.answer: Only the first statement is true, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.31.

gateAngle: Two shapes recur. One gives a sequence and asks which dependence of each kind exists (2024 Set 2 Q.31, 2015 Set 3 Q.47). The other asks abstractly which dependence is a hazard at all (2026 Set 1 Q.16, answer RAW). Both are answered by writing the read set and the write set of every instruction in program order.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In the same sequence, add I5: ADD R3, R1, R2 at the end. What new dependences on R3 appear, and which would matter in an out-of-order machine?
variations.why: It separates the true dependence from the name collisions, which is the point of the classification.
variations.answer: I4 reads R3 and I5 writes R3: WAR. I3 writes R3 and I5 writes R3: WAW. Neither stalls an in-order pipeline. In an out-of-order machine both could reorder into a wrong result and are removed by renaming R3 for I5; the true dependences I1 to I2 and I3 to I4 remain regardless.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is read-after-read never a hazard, however many instructions read the same register?
variations.why: It closes the obvious fourth case so that the student does not hesitate in the exam.
variations.answer: Because reading does not change the register: any number of readers can read the same value in any order and each gets the same answer. Nothing has to wait, and nothing can be wrong.

trap.what: Calling two writes to the same register a WAR because the pair looks reversed.
trap.why: WAR requires the earlier instruction to read; if both write, the dependence is WAW. Reading the earlier instruction's access first is the only reliable rule.
trap.counterexample: GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.31 option B calls I1 (writes R3) to I3 (writes R3) a WAR; it is WAW, and that is exactly why the option is false.

check.question: I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: MUL R7, R1, R3; I3: ADD R3, R2, R4. Name every dependence on R3.
check.answer: I1 writes and I2 reads R3: RAW. I2 reads and I3 writes R3: WAR. I1 writes and I3 writes: WAW.
check.explanation: One register, three accesses in the order write, read, write: the first pair is RAW, the second WAR, the outer pair WAW.

visual.title: Pipelining and Hazards
covers: read-after-write as the true dependence; a value flows
write-after-read as an anti-dependence; a name is reused
write-after-write as an output dependence; two writers
in an in-order five-stage pipeline only RAW causes a stall
